claim: In 2016, the US National Institutes of Health implemented a policy requiring investigators to consider sex as a biological variable.
source: In 2016, to address the historical overrepresentation of male subjects in biomedical research, the US National Institutes of Health implemented a policy requiring investigators to consider sex as a biological variable.
evidence: This is stated as a factual event in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction (Clayton and Collins, 2014).

claim: There was a significant increase in the proportion of studies that included both sexes across all nine disciplines between 2009 and 2019.
source: There was a significant increase in the proportion of studies that included both sexes across all nine disciplines, but in eight of the disciplines there was no change in the proportion studies that included data analyzed by sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bibliometric analysis data presented in the Results section and Figure 1A.

claim: In eight of the nine disciplines there was no change in the proportion of studies that included data analyzed by sex between 2009 and 2019.

claim: The majority of studies failed to provide rationale for single-sex studies or the lack of sex-based analyses.

evidence: This is supported by data showing only 30 out of 720 articles provided rationale, as described in the Results section.

claim: Studies that provided rationale for single-sex studies or lack of sex-based analyses relied on misconceptions surrounding the hormonal variability of females.

claim: Male subjects have been historically overrepresented in biomedical research.

claim: Male bias in research stems from the misconception that female animals increase experimental variability due to cyclical fluctuating hormones.
